summary: Discusses what an Internet standard data link protocol for point-to-point links should be able to do and how to judge candidates. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before picking a tool to connect two computers over a wire, you need to decide what it must do. This memo is that checklist.

questions: what are the requirements for a point-to-point protocol
what features does a point-to-point protocol need
what is an internet standard point-to-point protocol
subtitle: The 1989 checklist of what a standard protocol for point-to-point links had to do, and why every existing option fell short.

tldr.problem: Point-to-point serial links were common, but there was no agreed Internet Standard way to carry IP over them. Existing protocols were ad hoc or solved only narrow problems.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists 17 required features (such as framing, a protocol type field, error detection, liveness checks and option negotiation) and 7 non-requirements, then measures existing protocols against them.
tldr.outcome: Every protocol reviewed failed on key points. The author says this was the design requirements document of June 1989, followed for RFC 1134 through the time of publication in 1993.

facts.label: Liveness detection
facts.value: No more than a few minutes

today: RFC 1547 is an Informational memo from December 1993 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the requirements that, per its historical note, were followed from RFC 1134 onward.

sections.title: Why a Standard Was Needed
sections.content:
Most Internet hosts sat on LANs, with Ethernet the most common, or on X.25 style public data networks. Few used simple point-to-point links, even though serial links are among the oldest data communications methods and asynchronous RS-232 interfaces are almost everywhere.

One reason was the lack of a single agreed encapsulation protocol. There were plenty of non-standard ones and at least one de facto standard, Rick Adams' SLIP for BSD UNIX, which handles only the most rudimentary case: IP over asynchronous serial lines. The memo does not propose a design. It proposes requirements for an Internet Standard Point-to-Point Protocol (ISPPP), and any solutions it sketches are only examples.
sections.plainLanguage: People had many different ways to talk over a single cable, but nobody had agreed on one. This memo says what a good shared way should do.

sections.title: The Required Features
sections.content:
Section 2 lists 17 requirements. The core ones are: simplicity, transparency (data crosses the link unmodified, so framing characters in the data must be escaped or bit-stuffed), correct and efficient packet framing, low overhead (at most a few percent of raw bandwidth) and fast header processing.

The protocol must also multiplex many higher level protocols, so it needs a protocol type field. Eight bits are called too few; sixteen are suggested, although twelve bits (4096 protocols) should suffice. It must support many physical and data link types, including full duplex asynchronous RS-232 links with 8 data bits and no parity from 300 to 19.2k bps or more, and bit-oriented synchronous links such as RS-422, RS-423, V.35 and T1.

Other requirements cover basic error detection (a checksum or CRC, to avoid wasting bandwidth on corrupted packets), a standard default MTU of at least 1500 bytes per link type, support for switched and non-switched media, and symmetric operation with no fixed master and slave roles.
sections.plainLanguage: A good wire protocol must be simple, mark where each message starts and stops, say what kind of message it is, and notice if a message got scrambled.

sections.title: Link Health and Negotiation
sections.content:
Several requirements are about knowing the state of the link. A connection liveness mechanism must tell when a link is working and when it is defunct, discovering changes in no more than a few minutes. It should be on by default but can be disabled, for example when a public data network charges for traffic and constant pinging would cost money. Links start out "down" and are only declared "up" once both ends can send and receive.

The protocol must detect a looped-back link, as when a modem is placed in loopback for diagnosis, within one period of the liveness protocol. It must also detect misconfigured connections, such as swapped cables, by verifying the remote end's identity when possible. The goal is catching simple errors, not rigorous authentication.

Finally, it must allow negotiation of network layer addresses and of data compression, with algorithms guaranteed to terminate. Refusal to compress always wins over an offer. A general, extensible option negotiation protocol is the proposed route to cover these, plus MTU and encryption, and future needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends should check regularly that the cable really works both ways, notice if someone plugged it into the wrong place, and agree on settings like addresses before they start talking.

sections.title: Features Not Required
sections.content:
Section 3 says what the protocol does not have to do, as long as including it breaks no requirement. Error correction, flow control and sequencing are left to the transport layer; the data link need provide no more than IP's unreliable datagram service, and may even reorder packets. The protocol should not prevent error correction by private agreement on very noisy links.

It need not be backward compatible with other point-to-point protocols, support multi-point links, half-duplex or simplex links, or 7-bit asynchronous RS-232. A historical note adds that Switched Multimegabit Data Service, Frame Relay and Asynchronous Transfer Mode appeared since the original text, but are considerably more complex than the ISPPP.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo also lists jobs the wire protocol can skip, like making sure every message arrives in order, because other layers already do that.

sections.title: Prior Work Reviewed
sections.content:
Section 4 tests existing protocols against the list. SLIP is simple and transparent but has no protocol field, no error detection and no negotiation. RFC 916 (RATP) is far from simple and has no option negotiation or extensibility. The HDLC frame structure (ISO 3309) lacks multiplexing, standard MTUs and negotiation, yet the memo says its wide acceptance and simplicity may make it an ideal building block. Several vendor protocols (Cisco, Proteon, Ungermann Bass, Wellfleet) use HDLC framing with various type fields but lack option negotiation or fault detection.

The Xerox Network Systems synchronous protocol came closest, but it has only an 8-bit type field and misses the requirements on multiple data link protocols, fault detection and compression negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors tried each existing wire protocol against the checklist. None passed everything, though some had good parts to borrow.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content: The memo is Informational and defines no standard. Its abstract carries a historical note: this was the design requirements document dated June 1989, which was followed for RFC 1134 through the present, and it is published for completeness and future guidance. The security section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a record of the goals set at the start. It says nothing about security.
